idiom_name: chain of collection operations ended by a terminal operation
implementation_notes: Language-neutral form: represent the computation as an ordered sequence of operations that each accept a collection and return the next one (map/select, filter/where, flatMap/flatten, distinct, sort, group) and terminate with an operation that produces a single value (reduce/fold, collect, sum, count, find, any). Supply each operation's behaviour as a small pure function or function reference, keep the chain linear, and give it a name when it is reused. Decide the evaluation policy explicitly: an eager chain materialises one collection per stage and is easy to debug, whereas a lazy chain (views, iterators, sequences, streams) fuses the stages into one pass, can stop early and can read unbounded sources, but defers and reorders side effects. Use parallel variants (parallelStream, parallel, rayon, parallel collections) only when stages are stateless and associative, N*Q exceeds the parallelism threshold (typically N > 10,000 with non-trivial per-element cost Q), and the source is efficiently splittable (ArrayList, range, not LinkedList or BufferedReader). Prefer primitive specialised streams (IntStream, LongStream, DoubleStream) over boxed object streams for numeric aggregation to avoid per-element boxing allocations that can cost an order of magnitude in performance. Use teeing or fan-out collectors when the same pipeline must emit several independent aggregates in a single pass.
code_sketch:
names = users                       # source
      .filter(u -> u.active)        # stage: drop elements that fail the predicate
      .map(u -> u.email)            # stage: transform each element
      .distinct()                   # stage: remove duplicates
      .sorted()                     # stage: order
      .limit(10)                    # stage: short-circuit
      .collect(toList())            # terminal: materialise the result
pitfalls: Forgetting the terminal operation: a lazy chain does nothing until it is consumed, so stages with side effects silently never run.
Side effects inside stages make the pipeline order-dependent and unsafe under laziness and parallelism.
Reusing a consumed pipeline, or iterating a lazy chain twice, produces empty results or duplicated work.

sorted() before a short-circuiting terminal (findFirst/take) breaks laziness: sorted must see all upstream elements before emitting the first one, defeating the short-circuit. Use min()/max() instead, or sort after the short-circuit.

flatMap followed by findFirst does NOT short-circuit across sub-streams: each flatMap sub-stream is fully consumed before findFirst evaluates the next, so the pipeline can do far more work than expected.

Boxed numeric streams (Stream<Integer>) allocate a boxed object per element, costing roughly 10x more than IntStream for numeric aggregation. Always use primitive specialised streams for numeric work.
Parallel streams share the common ForkJoinPool: a long-running pipeline starves all other parallel work in the process. Use a custom ForkJoinPool with explicit thread count for isolation.
forEach on a parallel stream with a shared mutable collection (ArrayList, HashMap) is a data race that silently produces corrupted results. Use collect() with a proper thread-safe collector instead.

Stateful stages in a parallel pipeline (sorted, distinct without UNORDERED, limit) require buffering that limits parallelism and can introduce non-determinism unless the pipeline is explicitly unordered.
Two-argument toMap/collectByKey in production throws IllegalStateException on duplicate keys. Always use the three-argument overload that specifies a merge function.

Wrong move: chaining eager per-step operations (Elixir Enum.map/Enum.filter, a materialising list comprehension) over large or potentially infinite enumerables -> failure: every step traverses the whole source and materialises an intermediate list, so memory grows with the chain length and an infinite source never returns -> instead: compose the stages lazily (Elixir Stream, generator expressions, views) and trigger exactly one traversal with a terminal reduce/sum.

Wrong move: materialising a whole table with list()/collect() and then filtering and projecting in the pipeline -> failure: the database ships every row, memory grows with the table, and the filter runs after the fetch -> instead: push selection and projection down into the query (SQL WHERE, a lazy Spark DataFrame filter) so the pipeline only sees the rows that survive.

Wrong move: keeping multi-statement logic, mutable state or side effects inside inline lambdas so a loop fits on one fluent chain -> failure: the chain no longer reads as data flow, stages cannot be unit-tested or located in a stack trace, and readability drops below the loop it replaced (Effective Java Item 45: use streams judiciously, not for control flow that needs mutable state) -> instead: extract each stage's logic into a named, tested method the stage references, or keep the explicit loop when the step needs real control flow.
